summary.en: An **adjective** describes a noun (_a quiet street_) and goes after **be**, **look**, **feel**, **sound** and **seem**. An **adverb** describes a verb, an adjective or another adverb and often ends in **-ly** (_she spoke quietly_). English adjectives never take **-s**, and the adverb of **good** is **well**. Watch out for **hard / hardly**, **late / lately** and **fast**.
summary.es: Los adjetivos ingleses no concuerdan en plural: the important things, no the importants things. Después de look, feel y sound va adjetivo: You look tired, no You look tiredly.

form: Adjective + noun: _a difficult decision, two difficult decisions_ (no plural -s)
**be / look / feel / sound / seem / taste** + adjective: _The soup tastes wonderful._
Most adverbs: adjective + **-ly**: _careful → carefully, quick → quickly_; **-y → -ily**: _easy → easily_
Irregular: **good → well**; **hard, fast, late, early** are both adjective and adverb
Manner adverbs usually come **after the verb or its object**: _She drives carefully._ _He answered the question calmly._

uses.text: **Describe a noun** → adjective: _a reliable colleague_, _an exhausting journey_.
**Describe how something is, looks or feels** → adjective after a linking verb: _You seem stressed._ _That sounds interesting._
**Describe how an action is done** → adverb: _He reacted angrily._ _They played brilliantly._
**Strengthen an adjective or adverb** → very, really, extremely, fairly: _It was extremely cold._ _She works really hard._
**Same form, different meaning**: _hard_ (with effort) / _hardly_ (almost not); _late_ (not on time) / _lately_ (recently).

note.en: Hardly means almost not: _I hardly know him_ = I know him very little.

why.en: After look, feel, sound and seem we use an adjective, not an adverb.
why.es: Tras look / feel / sound / seem va adjetivo.

mistakes.wrong: These are very importants decisions, and the new rules are not clears.
mistakes.right: These are very important decisions, and the new rules are not clear.

why.en: Adjectives never take -s, even before or after a plural noun.
why.es: El adjetivo es invariable: no concuerda en plural.

mistakes.wrong: He speaks very good English and works hardly.
mistakes.right: He speaks very good English and works hard.

why.en: Hardly means almost not. The adverb of hard is hard.

mistakes.wrong: She plays the guitar very good.
mistakes.right: She plays the guitar very well.

why.en: Good is an adjective. The adverb is well.
why.es: Good es adjetivo; el adverbio es well.

mistakes.wrong: I speak well English and I like very much the food.
mistakes.right: I speak English well and I like the food very much.

why.en: Do not put an adverb between the verb and its object.
why.es: No se coloca el adverbio entre verbo y objeto.

examples.en: The new manager is friendly, but she seems quite nervous.
examples.es: La nueva jefa es amable, pero parece bastante nerviosa.

examples.en: Our flight arrived late because of the storm.
examples.es: Nuestro vuelo llegó tarde por la tormenta.

examples.en: That sounds like a sensible plan.
He drove carefully along the icy road.
I can hardly hear you; the line is terrible.
I've been feeling much better lately.
They worked hard all week, and the results were excellent.
He speaks fast, so I often ask him to slow down.

practice.prompt: You look ___ after the long flight.

explanation.en: Look is a linking verb here, so it takes an adjective.
The adverb of good is well.

practice.prompt: He worked ___ all night to finish the project.

explanation.en: Hard is both the adjective and the adverb. Hardly means almost not.

practice.prompt: I ___ understand what he said; the line was terrible.

explanation.en: Hardly means almost not, which is the meaning needed here.

practice.prompt: The manager spoke ___ about the delays.

explanation.en: We need an adverb to describe the verb spoke.
